{"id": "2af393a2-8147-4a5f-9f61-d2bf6ea7f5ff", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "You can still do this. You don't need historical scores for the old prompt. If you still have its exact text, you can score it today on the same inputs as the new one. A head-to-head run on one fixed dataset is also a stronger comparison than old scores from a different time and traffic mix.

**How to set it up**
1. **Build one fixed test set.** Use a few hundred real inputs, ideally sampled from production. If Bedrock invocation logging is on, you can pull them from there. Add known edge cases and past failures. Freeze the set and don't change it between runs.
2. **Run both prompts on that set.** Keep everything else the same: model and version, temperature, max tokens, and any retrieval or knowledge base setup. Only the prompt should differ.
3. **Score both with the same method.**
   - Use a Bedrock evaluation job with the same judge model and the same metrics for both prompts. Bedrock model evaluation supports automated (LLM-as-judge) and human scoring. If you use RAG, there is a separate RAG evaluation type on knowledge bases.
   - Compare the two prompts on the same inputs, not just on overall averages.
4. **Add a human review on a sample.** This matters most for subjective or customer-facing quality. LLM judges have known blind spots, so one judge number isn't proof. Include a safety dimension too.
5. **Check for noise before you claim a win.** Judge scores can swing between runs. Run each prompt more than once. Look at the standard error and confidence bounds, and only call it better if the gap is clearly larger than the noise.
6. **Compare the side effects.** Look at the finish-reason mix. A rise in `max_tokens` cutoffs is a quality regression that latency and error metrics won't show. Also compare token cost and latency.

**Make it repeatable**
- Save the dataset, prompts, judge settings, and scores in a versioned place, such as S3 or a repo.
- Publish the scores as metrics.
- Define a pass threshold for new prompts. AWS publishes no universal number, so it has to come from your workload. Make a regression block promotion.

**Limits to keep in mind**
- You can score old production outputs from the logs, but that is a different input mix from the new run. Use it as a sanity check, not as the baseline.
- If the old prompt's exact text and settings are lost, you can't rebuild a faithful baseline. Best-effort reconstruction would weaken the claim.

If you'd like, I can check your account for existing evaluation jobs and whether invocation logging is enabled. That would tell us whether you can build the test set from real traffic today. Tell me the region and the model or knowledge base involved.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
